claim: Cancer poses danger because of its unregulated growth, development of resistance, and metastatic spread to vital organs.
source: Cancer poses danger because of its unregulated growth, development of resistance, and metastatic spread to vital organs.
evidence: This is a general statement about cancer characteristics presented in the abstract without specific supporting data in the manuscript.

claim: Prevention generally results in more positive therapeutic outcomes than post-diagnostic interventions.
source: Whereas prevention generally results in more positive therapeutic outcomes than post-diagnostic interventions, this advantage is substantially lowered should prevention initially fail to arrest tumour growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by numerical simulations and analytical results presented in Figures 3, 4, and 5.

claim: The advantage of prevention over post-diagnostic intervention is substantially lowered should prevention initially fail to arrest tumour growth.
source: Whereas prevention generally results in more positive therapeutic outcomes than post-diagnostic interventions, this advantage is substantially lowered should prevention initially fail to arrest tumour growth.
evidence: This is supported by simulation results showing that failed prevention leads to residual populations with more resistant clones.

claim: Natural selection for increases in tumour cell population growth can be represented as the net effect of increased cell division rates and/or decreased apoptosis.
source: Natural selection for increases in tumour cell population growth can be represented as the net effect of increased cell division rates and/or decreased apoptosis (e.g., Wodarz and Komarova, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Wodarz and Komarova, 2007.

claim: Relatively rare driver mutations confer a net growth advantage.
source: Relatively rare driver mutations confer such a net growth advantage, whereas numerically dominant passenger mutations with initially neutral or mildly deleterious effects (Marusyk et al., 2012; Bozic et al., 2013; McFarland et al., 2013) can increase in frequency due to genetic hitchhiking or subsequent positive selection.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on driver and passenger mutations.

claim: Passenger mutations with initially neutral or mildly deleterious effects can increase in frequency due to genetic hitchhiking or subsequent positive selection.
source: Relatively rare driver mutations confer such a net growth advantage, whereas numerically dominant passenger mutations with initially neutral or mildly deleterious effects (Marusyk et al., 2012; Bozic et al., 2013; McFarland et al., 2013) can increase in frequency due to genetic hitchhiking or subsequent positive selection.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Marusyk et al., 2012; Bozic et al., 2013; McFarland et al., 2013.

claim: Sufficiently large tumours could contain different clones that, taken as a group, can resist some, if not most, chemotherapies.
source: Amongst the many passengers in a growing tumour, some can contribute to chemoresistance, and sufficiently large tumours could contain different clones that, taken as a group, can resist some, if not most, chemotherapies (see Michor et al., 2005 for resistance to imatinib).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Michor et al., 2005 regarding resistance to imatinib.

claim: Chemotherapeutic remission followed by relapse suggests that resistant cells are often present at low frequencies prior to therapy.
source: Chemotherapeutic remission followed by relapse suggests that these resistant cells are often present at low frequencies prior to therapy, either due to genetic drift or costs associated with resistance.
evidence: This is an inference based on clinical observations of remission and relapse patterns.

claim: MTD is particularly prone to select for chemoresistance.
source: This body of work indicates that MTD is particularly prone to select for chemoresistance (e.g., Foo and Michor, 2009; Foo and Michor, 2010; Lorz et al., 2013), and what little empirical work exists supports this basic prediction (Turke et al., 2010), but see (Kouyos et al., 2014) for other disease systems.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to theoretical work (Foo and Michor, 2009; Foo and Michor, 2010; Lorz et al., 2013) and empirical work (Turke et al., 2010).

claim: Empirical work supports the prediction that MTD is prone to select for chemoresistance.
source: This body of work indicates that MTD is particularly prone to select for chemoresistance (e.g., Foo and Michor, 2009; Foo and Michor, 2010; Lorz et al., 2013), and what little empirical work exists supports this basic prediction (Turke et al., 2010), but see (Kouyos et al., 2014) for other disease systems.
evidence: This is supported by citation to empirical work by Turke et al., 2010.

claim: The evolutionary rate and associated emergence of a diversity of chemoresistant lineages is a major determinant in the success or failure of multiple drugs vs a single one.
source: They showed that the evolutionary rate and associated emergence of a diversity of chemoresistant lineages is a major determinant in the success or failure of multiple drugs vs a single one.
evidence: This refers to findings from Komarova and Wodarz (2005) cited in the previous sentence.

claim: Combination strategies of cytotoxic and cytostatic therapies could be designed to be superior in terms of tumour eradication or managing resistance than either agent used alone.
source: Lorz and co-workers (Lorz et al., 2013) recently modelled the employment of cytotoxic and cytostatic therapies alone or in combination and showed how combination strategies could be designed to be superior in terms of tumour eradication or managing resistance than either agent used alone.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lorz et al., 2013.

claim: Drugs slowing the generation of chemoresistant mutants and subsequent evolution are more likely to be successful than those only increasing cell death rates.
source: One of their main conclusions is that drugs slowing the generation of chemoresistant mutants and subsequent evolution are more likely to be successful than those only increasing cell death rates.
evidence: This refers to conclusions from Foo and Michor (2009) cited in the previous sentence.

claim: All individuals harbour pre-cancerous lesions, some of which may transform into invasive carcinoma.
source: In depth consideration of preventive measures and their likely impact on individual risk and epidemiological trends is important given the likelihood that all individuals harbour pre-cancerous lesions, some of which may transform into invasive carcinoma (Bissell and Hines, 2011; Greaves, 2014), and concerns as to whether technological advances will continue to make significant headway in treating clinically detected cancers (Gillies et al., 2012; Vogelstein et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bissell and Hines, 2011; Greaves, 2014.

claim: The model assumes that an individual can contract at most a single cancer, originating from a single lesion.
source: We assume that an individual can contract at most a single cancer, originating from a single lesion.
evidence: This is a stated assumption of the modeling framework.

claim: The expected mean tumour size in a population of subjects can be substantially different from the median, since the former is highly influenced by outliers due to tumours of very large size.
source: Specifically, we show that the expected mean tumour size in a population of subjects can be substantially different from the median, since the former is highly influenced by outliers due to tumours of very large size.
evidence: This is supported by analytical and numerical results shown in Appendix 1—figure 1B.

claim: Treatment outcome is sensitive to initial conditions, particularly for intermediate-sized tumours.
source: We then consider constant preventive measures and show that treatment outcome is sensitive to initial conditions, particularly for intermediate-sized tumours.
evidence: This is supported by numerical simulations presented in the Results section.

claim: Higher impacts on the cancer cell population are usually required for post-diagnostic interventions to achieve a level of control comparable to prevention.
source: We show as expected that therapeutic outcomes are generally superior under prevention vs post-diagnostic intervention, and that higher impacts on the cancer cell population are usually required for post-diagnostic interventions to achieve a level of control comparable to prevention.
evidence: This is supported by comparative numerical simulations shown in Figures 3, 4, and 5.

claim: Should resection leave sufficiently large numbers of residual cells (or metastases are not discovered), then a range of the most successful outcomes under prevention is not attainable under post-diagnostic intervention, regardless of potential cell arrest.
source: Moreover, we find that should resection leave sufficiently large numbers of residual cells (or metastases are not discovered), then a range of the most successful outcomes under prevention is not attainable under post-diagnostic intervention, regardless of potential cell arrest.
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 5.

claim: There is little gained in terms of outcomes in post-diagnostic intervention beyond approximately 0.3% cell arrest per day for both small (10,000) and large (1 million) cancer cell populations.
source: Finally and importantly, whereas there is little gained in terms of outcomes in post-diagnostic intervention beyond approximately 0.3% cell arrest per day for both small (10,000) and large (1 million) cancer cell populations, prevention outcomes may achieve continual gains for the latter cell number, up to about 0.6% cell arrest per day.
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Prevention outcomes may achieve continual gains for large (1 million) cancer cell populations, up to about 0.6% cell arrest per day.
source: Finally and importantly, whereas there is little gained in terms of outcomes in post-diagnostic intervention beyond approximately 0.3% cell arrest per day for both small (10,000) and large (1 million) cancer cell populations, prevention outcomes may achieve continual gains for the latter cell number, up to about 0.6% cell arrest per day.
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A mean field approach assumes a large initial number of cells and averages any effects of stochasticity.
source: A mean field approach assumes a large initial number of cells (Krapivsky et al., 2010) and averages any effects of stochasticity, so that an intermediate state of the system is described by a set of ordinary differential equations (i.e., master equations; Gardiner, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Krapivsky et al., 2010 and Gardiner, 2004.

claim: The fitness function fij is defined by the number of accumulated drivers (i = 0, 1, …, N) and resistance status (j = 0, 1).
source: The fitness function fij, the difference between the birth and death rates of a cell, is defined by the number of accumulated drivers (i = 0, 1, …, N) and resistance status (j = 0, 1): a sensitive cancerous cell with a single driver has selective advantage s, and any accumulated driver adds s to fitness, while resistance is associated with a constant cost c.
evidence: This is a definition of the model's fitness function.

claim: A sensitive cancerous cell with a single driver has selective advantage s, and any accumulated driver adds s to fitness.
source: The fitness function fij, the difference between the birth and death rates of a cell, is defined by the number of accumulated drivers (i = 0, 1, …, N) and resistance status (j = 0, 1): a sensitive cancerous cell with a single driver has selective advantage s, and any accumulated driver adds s to fitness, while resistance is associated with a constant cost c.
evidence: This is a stated assumption of the model.

claim: Resistance is associated with a constant cost c.
source: The fitness function fij, the difference between the birth and death rates of a cell, is defined by the number of accumulated drivers (i = 0, 1, …, N) and resistance status (j = 0, 1): a sensitive cancerous cell with a single driver has selective advantage s, and any accumulated driver adds s to fitness, while resistance is associated with a constant cost c.
evidence: This is a stated assumption of the model.

claim: Exposure to a single treatment affects only non-resistant cells (j = 0), incurring a loss σ to their fitness.
source: Exposure to a single treatment affects only non-resistant cells (j = 0), incurring a loss σ to their fitness.
evidence: This is a stated assumption of the model.

claim: The assumption of driver additivity is a special case of multiplicative fitness, and both are approximately equivalent for very small s.
source: The assumption of driver additivity is a special case of multiplicative fitness, and both are approximately equivalent for very small s.
evidence: This is a mathematical statement about the model assumptions.

claim: There is an excellent correspondence between analytical and numerical results for σ varied in range of s.
source: There is an excellent correspondence between analytical and numerical results for σ varied in range of s (Appendix 1—figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of analytical and numerical results shown in Appendix 1—figure 1A.

claim: The mean diverges considerably from median behaviour in the majority of cases, since the former is strongly influenced by outliers with high-tumour cell numbers.
source: A more detailed study of the distribution of tumour sizes reveals that the mean diverges considerably from median behaviour in the majority of cases, since the former is strongly influenced by outliers with high-tumour cell numbers (see Appendix 1—figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Appendix 1—figure 1B.

claim: An untreated tumour reaches the assumed detection threshold of 10^9 cells by about 18 years on average.
source: An untreated tumour reaches the assumed detection threshold of 109 cells by about 18 years on average and because it is not subject to strong negative selection (we assume low c), any emerging resistant cell-lines are likely to remain at low frequency (0.03% at the detection time in the example of Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by numerical simulation results shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In an untreated tumour, any emerging resistant cell-lines are likely to remain at low frequency (0.03% at the detection time).
source: An untreated tumour reaches the assumed detection threshold of 109 cells by about 18 years on average and because it is not subject to strong negative selection (we assume low c), any emerging resistant cell-lines are likely to remain at low frequency (0.03% at the detection time in the example of Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by numerical simulation results shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Low-treatment intensity delays tumour growth and thus time of detection by approximately 16 years.
source: In Figure 1B, low-treatment intensity delays tumour growth and thus time of detection by approximately 16 years, while an increase in dose tends to result in tumours dominated by resistant cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by numerical simulation results shown in Figure 1B.

claim: An increase in dose tends to result in tumours dominated by resistant cells.
source: In Figure 1B, low-treatment intensity delays tumour growth and thus time of detection by approximately 16 years, while an increase in dose tends to result in tumours dominated by resistant cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by numerical simulation results shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Resistant cell populations are sometimes observed to go extinct stemming from stochasticity, and this tends to occur more at high-treatment levels.
source: Despite being unaffected by treatment, resistant cell populations are sometimes observed to go extinct stemming from stochasticity (Figure 1D), and this tends to occur more at high-treatment levels, because there are fewer sensitive tumour cells to seed new (mutant) resistant cell populations.
evidence: This is supported by numerical simulation results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Tumour growth is largely driven by its non-resistant part for relatively low-impact treatments σ < 2s.
source: The magnitude of the selective advantage s shows that tumour growth is largely driven by its non-resistant part for relatively low-impact treatments σ < 2s (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The tumour shifts from being mainly non-resistant to resistant at σ ≈ 2s.
source: Importantly, the tumour shifts from being mainly non-resistant to resistant at σ ≈ 2s, which is reflected by the inflection point in the trajectory of the median (indicated by point B in Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Detection times are most variable at σ ≈ 2s.
source: Notice that detection times are also most variable at σ ≈ 2s.
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The median changes smoothly at high-treatment levels (σ > 2s), tending to a horizontal asymptote.
source: The median changes smoothly at high-treatment levels (σ > 2s), tending to a horizontal asymptote.
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: At high-treatment levels, the dynamics are strongly influenced by the actual time point at which the first resistance mutation occurs.
source: This is explained by the fact that the sensitive part is heavily suppressed at high-treatment levels, meaning that the dynamics are strongly influenced by the actual time point at which the first resistance mutation occurs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model dynamics and numerical results.

claim: Early-detected tumours are more likely to be resistant under constant treatments than those detected at later times.
source: We find, counterintuitively, that early-detected tumours are more likely to be resistant under constant treatments than those detected at later times (A, B, and C in Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Tumours under treatment that by chance obtain resistance early grow faster than those that do not.
source: This is because tumours under treatment that by chance obtain resistance early grow faster than those that do not.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model dynamics explaining the counterintuitive finding.

claim: By the time of detection, non-resistant tumours usually accumulate up to 4 additional drivers on average, while resistant tumours have fewer.
source: By the time of detection, non-resistant tumours usually accumulate up to 4 additional drivers on average, while resistant tumours have fewer.
evidence: This is supported by numerical simulation results.

claim: The inflection point at σ ≈ 2s in Figure 2A is due to the accumulation of additional drivers within tumours and associated increases in the likelihood that the tumour eventually resists treatment.
source: The inflection point at σ ≈ 2s in Figure 2A is due to the accumulation of additional drivers within tumours and associated increases in the likelihood that the tumour eventually resists treatment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model dynamics and numerical results.

claim: A tumour can be suppressed only if σ > 2s when the initial population consists of 10^6 cells and a mutant cell with one additional driver and associated fitness 2s appears very rapidly.
source: Since the initial population consists of 106 cells, in the absence of treatment, a mutant cell with one additional driver and associated fitness 2s will appear very rapidly. Such a tumour can be suppressed only if σ > 2s.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model dynamics.

claim: The inflection point σ ≈ 2s disappears when N = 0 (no additional driver mutations allowed).
source: This is supported by additional numerical experiments where we vary the maximal number of additional driver mutations N: the inflection point σ ≈ 2s disappears when N = 0 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The initial cancer cell number M0 affects both the median and distribution of detection times.
source: The initial cancer cell number M0 affects both the median and distribution of detection times (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: For large initial tumours, growth is deterministic and exponential.
source: For large initial tumours, growth is deterministic and exponential.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model dynamics and numerical results.

claim: A tumour is likely to be eradicated under a range of constant treatments when M0 = 10^5 or fewer initial cells.
source: Moreover, we find that a tumour is likely to be eradicated under a range of constant treatments when M0 = 105 or fewer initial cells; in contrast, a tumour is virtually certain to persist regardless of treatment level for M0 = 107 cells or greater (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: A tumour is virtually certain to persist regardless of treatment level for M0 = 10^7 cells or greater.
source: Moreover, we find that a tumour is likely to be eradicated under a range of constant treatments when M0 = 105 or fewer initial cells; in contrast, a tumour is virtually certain to persist regardless of treatment level for M0 = 107 cells or greater (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Tumours that are c. 1% the size of most clinically detectable, internal cancers will typically be impossible to eradicate by single molecule chemoprevention when resistance is possible.
source: In other words, our model indicates that tumours that are c. 1% the size of most clinically detectable, internal cancers will typically be impossible to eradicate by single molecule chemoprevention when resistance is possible.
evidence: This is an inference based on the numerical results showing that tumours with 10^7 cells or more cannot be eradicated.

claim: Many tumours with 1 million cells will either already contain or rapidly subsequently acquire resistant cells.
source: Given the mutation rates assumed here, many tumours with 1 million cells will either already contain or rapidly subsequently acquire resistant cells (Iwasa et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Iwasa et al., 2006 and the mutation rates used in the model.

claim: The initial fraction of resistant cells in a tumour has little impact on dynamics.
source: It is therefore not surprising that the initial fraction of resistant cells in a tumour has little impact on dynamics (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The fraction of persons with tumours that remain undetected after 50 years of growth improves substantially with lower numbers of initial resistance mutations, particularly at higher treatment levels.
source: In contrast, another measure of success in control (the fraction of persons with tumours that remain undetected after 50 years of growth) improves substantially with lower numbers of initial resistance mutations, particularly at higher treatment levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Tumours exhibit more or less deterministic growth depending on the initial number of cells M0 and driver mutation rate u.
source: We find that tumours exhibit more or less deterministic growth depending on the initial number of cells M0 and driver mutation rate u whereby the larger the population (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) or the higher the mutation rate (Appendix 1—figure 4A), the less apparent are stochastic effects.
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and Appendix 1—figure 4A.

claim: Under dose-dependent costs, a drug treatment only applied when the number of non-resistant cells exceeds the number of resistant cells leads to slower long-term tumour growth than does a constant therapy.
source: Numerical studies presented in more detail in 'A simple form of drug addiction for resistant cell-lines' in Appendix 1 show that under dose-dependent costs, a drug treatment only applied when the number of non-resistant cells exceeds the number of resistant cells (e.g., a metronomic therapy [Fischer et al., 2015]) leads to slower long-term tumour growth than does a constant therapy.
evidence: This is supported by numerical studies presented in Appendix 1.

claim: Early discovery (at 10^9 cells) yields an additional 3.4 years compared to late discovery (at 10^11 cells) at σ = 1.5%.
source: Comparing the median expectations of years from tumour excision to relapse, early discovery (at 109 cells) yields an additional 3.4 years compared to late discovery (at 1011 cells) at σ = 1.5% (medians for low vs high detection thresholds are 14.8 and 11.4 years, respectively; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 20 years after resection and commencing treatment, the probability of tumour non-detection is close to zero, regardless of treatment intensity, when post-diagnostic resection leaves 10^6 cells.
source: Consider the following example: 20 years after resection and commencing treatment, the probability of tumour non-detection (i.e., the tumour is either eradicated or does not reach the detection threshold) is close to zero, regardless of treatment intensity (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: For prevention starting at 10^6 cells that fails to control the incipient tumour for 50 years, the detection time is substantially longer than either of the excision cases (median 25.5 years for σ = 1.5%).
source: Contrast this with cases of prevention starting at the same cancer cell population size (106 cells) but which fail to control the incipient tumour for the 50 years of the simulation: the detection time of these potentially life-threatening tumours is substantially longer than either of the excision cases (median 25.5 years for σ = 1.5%, i.e., 0.3–0.4% potential cell arrest per day), and tumours are managed below the detection threshold after 20 years in more than 80% of cases for any σ > 1.0% (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: For prevention starting at 10^6 cells, tumours are managed below the detection threshold after 20 years in more than 80% of cases for any σ > 1.0%.
source: Contrast this with cases of prevention starting at the same cancer cell population size (106 cells) but which fail to control the incipient tumour for the 50 years of the simulation: the detection time of these potentially life-threatening tumours is substantially longer than either of the excision cases (median 25.5 years for σ = 1.5%, i.e., 0.3–0.4% potential cell arrest per day), and tumours are managed below the detection threshold after 20 years in more than 80% of cases for any σ > 1.0% (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: When there are 10^4 residual cells, stochastic effects play a more important role in dynamics.
source: Now consider a residual population of 1/100th the previous case, that is, 104 cells. Here, stochastic effects play a more important role in dynamics (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The secondary detection times are more variable for small initial tumours compared to larger ones.
source: Interestingly, the secondary detection times (i.e., when residual or metastatic cells grow to form a new tumour) are more variable for small initial tumours compared to larger ones (cf the median 35.8 years, 90% CIs [17.0, 70.5] years vs 22.4, [13.7, 37.0] years for 109 vs 1011, respectively, with σ = 1.5%).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results comparing different initial tumour sizes.

claim: For both thresholds of tumour excision, subsequent cancer cell arrest levels beyond approximately σ = 1.5% make little difference in terms of tumour growth.
source: Importantly, for both thresholds of tumour excision, subsequent cancer cell arrest levels beyond approximately σ = 1.5% make little difference in terms of tumour growth (Figure 3B-D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D), since virtually all of the sensitive cells post-excision will be arrested or killed by the measure beyond this level, leaving uncontrollable resistant cells to grow and repopulate the primary tumour site and/or metastases.
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 3B-D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: For post-diagnostic interventions, knowledge about the number of drivers at the time of tumour discovery is a far better predictor of outcome than information about the time from tumour initiation to discovery.
source: Moreover, we find that for post-diagnostic interventions knowledge about the number of drivers at the time of tumour discovery is a far better predictor of outcome than information about the time from tumour initiation to discovery, and that increases in treatment intensity tend to decrease predictive accuracy (Figure 3—figure supplements 2–5).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 2–5.

claim: Increases in treatment intensity tend to decrease predictive accuracy of outcome for post-diagnostic interventions.
source: Moreover, we find that for post-diagnostic interventions knowledge about the number of drivers at the time of tumour discovery is a far better predictor of outcome than information about the time from tumour initiation to discovery, and that increases in treatment intensity tend to decrease predictive accuracy (Figure 3—figure supplements 2–5).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 2–5.

claim: When prevention starts at relatively large cancer cell populations (1 million cells), only small comparative gains occur from higher cell arrest in terms of outright treatment success.
source: When prevention starts at (or tumour resection misses) relatively large cancer cell populations (1 million cells), only small comparative gains occur from higher cell arrest in terms of outright treatment success (Figure 5A), whereas interventions starting at much smaller cancer cell numbers (10,000) result in considerably greater outright success (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Interventions starting at much smaller cancer cell numbers (10,000) result in considerably greater outright success.
source: When prevention starts at (or tumour resection misses) relatively large cancer cell populations (1 million cells), only small comparative gains occur from higher cell arrest in terms of outright treatment success (Figure 5A), whereas interventions starting at much smaller cancer cell numbers (10,000) result in considerably greater outright success (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Prevention generally results in superior outcomes in terms of delaying tumour growth, particularly for large residual cell populations.
source: Looking at situations of relapse only for prevention vs post-diagnostic intervention, the former generally results in superior outcomes in terms of delaying tumour growth, particularly for large residual cell populations (cf Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: For lower numbers of residual cells, some post-diagnostic resected tumours in the sample will be initially resistance free.
source: In contrast, for lower numbers of residual cells, some post-diagnostic resected tumours in the sample will be initially resistance free (cf Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Prior selection for resistance in initially failed prevention generally results in larger residual resistant cell populations than pre-therapeutic residual populations in post-diagnostic situations.
source: Prior selection for resistance in initially failed prevention generally results in larger residual resistant cell populations than pre-therapeutic residual populations in post-diagnostic situations (filled bars, cf captions A and B in Figure 5—figure supplements 2, 3), but smaller residual resistant cell populations than treatment failures following post-diagnostic resection (hatched bars, cf captions A and D in Figure 5—figure supplements 2, 3).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 2, 3.

claim: Secondary failures are associated with larger percentages of resistant subclones and a shift in the distributions towards more drivers.
source: Note that, as expected, secondary failures are associated with larger percentages of resistant subclones and a shift in the distributions towards more drivers (cf captions C and D in Figure 5—figure supplements 2, 3).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 2, 3.

claim: For large cancer cell populations (1 million cells), treating preventively at levels beyond about 0.3% arrest per day increases median delays in detection times due to outright success but has no effect on the lower 95th percentile.
source: We see that when both non-relapse (Figure 5A) and relapse (Figure 5C) are taken into account for large cancer cell populations (1 million cells), treating preventively at levels beyond about 0.3% arrest per day increases median delays in detection times due to outright success (i.e., survival beyond 50 years) but has no effect on the lower 95th percentile (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Arrest beyond approximately 0.6% per day does not yield further gains for prevention of large cancer cell populations.
source: (Although not shown, arrest beyond approximately 0.6% per day does not yield further gains).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from numerical simulations not shown in the figures.

claim: Post-diagnostic intervention improves only marginally beyond daily arrest levels of about 0.3% for large cancer cell populations.
source: In contrast, post-diagnostic intervention improves only marginally beyond daily arrest levels of about 0.3% (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 5E.

claim: For smaller cancer cell populations (10,000), a high median probability of full success is obtained >0.1% and >0.3% daily arrest for prevention and post-diagnostic intervention, respectively.
source: Figure 5F shows the corresponding results for smaller cancer cell populations (based on integrating the results in Figure 5B,D), whereby a high median probability of full success is obtained >0.1% and >0.3% daily arrest for prevention and post-diagnostic intervention, respectively (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Beyond low impact thresholds—approximated by the Darwinian fitness of the subclone with the most driver mutations—little additional control is achieved when resistant subclones are present or likely to emerge.
source: Our central result is that beyond low impact thresholds—approximated by the Darwinian fitness of the subclone with the most driver mutations—little additional control is achieved when resistant subclones are present or likely to emerge during the long-term intervention assumed here.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding supported by multiple numerical results throughout the manuscript.

claim: To achieve a given outcome, prevention requires smaller effects on cancer cell populations of a given size than do post-diagnostic interventions.
source: We found that, as expected, to achieve a given outcome, prevention requires smaller effects on cancer cell populations of a given size than do post-diagnostic interventions, the latter having smaller probabilities of complete cure and shorter times to tumour relapse.
evidence: This is a summary finding supported by numerical results in Figures 3, 4, and 5.

claim: For any given cell arrest level, prevention is, on average, superior to comparable post-diagnostic interventions, even when including cases where prevention initially fails.
source: Inversely and importantly, for any given cell arrest level, prevention is, on average, superior to comparable post-diagnostic interventions, even when including cases where prevention initially fails, and resection and additional therapy are needed.
evidence: This is a summary finding supported by numerical results in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Maximal long-term control occurs at surprisingly low daily levels of arrest: approximately 0.6% and 0.3% for preventive and post-diagnostic interventions, respectively, for interventions targeting 1 million cancer cells.
source: Specifically, based on empirical parameter estimates, we find that maximal long-term control occurs at surprisingly low daily levels of arrest. In the example where interventions target 1 million cancer cells, these levels are approximately 0.6% and 0.3% for preventive and post-diagnostic interventions, respectively.
evidence: This is a summary finding supported by numerical results in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Should prevention initially fail and a tumour be diagnosed and resected, any residual or metastatic cells are likely to contain more resistant clones than the corresponding situation for a post-diagnostic tumour.
source: However, should prevention initially fail and a tumour be diagnosed and resected, any residual or metastatic cells are likely to contain more resistant clones than the corresponding situation for a post-diagnostic tumour.
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 2, 3.

claim: Low impact interventions risk being unable to control subclones with the most fitness-enhancing drivers, whereas high levels of arrest risk selecting for resistance.
source: Our results point to what is perhaps an underappreciated challenge in cancer control: low impact interventions risk being unable to control subclones with the most fitness-enhancing drivers, whereas high levels of arrest risk selecting for resistance (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a summary inference supported by numerical results throughout the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Chemopreventive therapies are uncommon, despite empirical support for their effects.
source: Whereas primary prevention is becoming an increasingly significant approach in reducing risk of certain cancers (e.g., Colditz and Bohlke, 2014), chemopreventive therapies are uncommon, despite empirical support for their effects (William et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to William et al., 2009.

claim: Low doses of verapamil and 2-deoxyglucose could be administered adaptively to promote longer tumour progression times.
source: For example, Silva and colleagues (Silva et al., 2012) parameterized computational models to show how low doses of verapamil and 2-deoxyglucose could be administered adaptively to promote longer tumour progression times.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Silva et al., 2012.

claim: Mice commencing NSAID treatment at 4 weeks of age had significantly smaller tumour masses and more survived to the end of the experiment than controls or those commencing treatment at an older age.
source: They showed that mice commencing the treatment at 4 weeks of age had significantly smaller tumour masses, and that more survived to the end of the experiment than either the controls or those mice commencing the treatment at an older age.
evidence: This refers to findings from Ibrahim-Hashim et al., 2012 cited in the previous sentence.

claim: NSAID use in people with Barrett's oesophagus is associated with reductions in somatic genomic abnormalities and their growth to detectable levels.
source: Kostadinov et al. (2013) showed how NSAID use in a sample of people with Barrett's oesophagus is associated with reductions in somatic genomic abnormalities and their growth to detectable levels.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kostadinov et al., 2013.

claim: It is not known to what extent reductions in cancer progression under NSAIDs are due to either cytotoxic or cytostatic effects or both.
source: It is noteworthy that it is not known to what extent reductions in cancer progression under NSAIDs are due to either cytotoxic or cytostatic effects or both.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge regarding NSAID mechanisms.

claim: Studies have argued that metastatic potential rather than tumour size may be a better predictor of future survival.
source: Due caution is necessary in interpreting our results, since studies have argued that metastatic potential rather than tumour size may be a better predictor of future survival (Hynes, 2003; Foulkes et al., 2010; Sethi and Kang, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hynes, 2003; Foulkes et al., 2010; Sethi and Kang, 2011.

claim: Prevention typically confronts smaller, less heterogeneous neoplasms, which are less likely to have resistant clones and to have metastasised.
source: However, given the expectation that prevention typically confronts smaller, less heterogeneous neoplasms, which are less likely to have resistant clones and to have metastasised (Hochberg et al., 2013; Gerlinger et al., 2014), support our basic conclusion that prevention is generally a superior strategy in terms of cancer-free survival compared to post-diagnostic intervention.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hochberg et al., 2013; Gerlinger et al., 2014.

claim: Several alternative approaches to MTD have been proposed where the objective is to manage rather than eradicate tumours.
source: Over the past decade, several alternative approaches to MTD have been proposed, where the objective is to manage rather than eradicate tumours (e.g., Maley et al., 2004; Komarova and Wodarz, 2005; Gatenby, 2009; Gatenby et al., 2009a, 2009b; Foo and Michor, 2010; Jansen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on tumour management approaches.

claim: Tumours typically achieve several additional driver mutations by the time they reach detection.
source: We found that tumours typically achieve several additional driver mutations by the time they reach detection (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; Figure 5—figure supplements 2, 3), which approximates certain estimates (Stratton et al., 2009) but falls short of others (Sjoblom et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by numerical results shown in Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 5—figure supplements 2, 3.

claim: The two most important variables in determining therapeutic outcome are the size of the initial cancer cell population and associated tumour heterogeneity in terms of accumulated drivers and the presence of resistance phenotypes.
source: Our results indicate that the two most important variables in determining therapeutic outcome are (1) the size of the initial cancer cell population (i.e., when prevention commences and/or post-diagnosis, following resection), (2) associated tumour heterogeneity in terms of accumulated drivers, and the presence of resistance phenotypes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on numerical results throughout the manuscript.

claim: If order-of-magnitude estimates of cell populations and intra-tumour heterogeneity are possible, then low dose, continuous, constant approaches could be established that lower and possibly minimize risks of the emergence of future, life-threatening cancers.
source: We suggest that if order-of-magnitude estimates of cell populations and intra-tumour heterogeneity are possible, then low dose, continuous, constant approaches could be established that lower and possibly minimize risks of the emergence of future, life-threatening cancers.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the modeling results.

claim: Low dose, continuous approaches will generally be superior to more aggressive chemotherapies if therapeutic resistance is a risk factor.
source: According to our model, such options will generally be superior to more aggressive chemotherapies if therapeutic resistance is a risk factor.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the modeling results throughout the manuscript.

claim: The main hurdle to post-diagnostic MTD interventions remains resistant subclones.
source: Our study nevertheless predicts that the main hurdle to post-diagnostic MTD interventions remains resistant subclones, since beyond minimal impacts on the order of 0.3% per day for the larger of the two residual or metastatic cell populations simulated here (which are still very small by clinical diagnostic standards—c 1 mm3), increased therapeutic intensity selects disproportionally for resistance and has negligible benefits in terms of delaying life-threatening cancers.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on numerical results in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Beyond minimal impacts on the order of 0.3% per day for residual populations of 1 million cells, increased therapeutic intensity selects disproportionally for resistance and has negligible benefits in terms of delaying life-threatening cancers.
source: Our study nevertheless predicts that the main hurdle to post-diagnostic MTD interventions remains resistant subclones, since beyond minimal impacts on the order of 0.3% per day for the larger of the two residual or metastatic cell populations simulated here (which are still very small by clinical diagnostic standards—c 1 mm3), increased therapeutic intensity selects disproportionally for resistance and has negligible benefits in terms of delaying life-threatening cancers.
evidence: This is supported by numerical results in Figures 3 and 5.
